sections.title: Functions package behavior
sections.body: A function gives a reusable name to a calculation or action. Its inputs are parameters, the supplied values are arguments, and return sends a result to the caller. A small function with one clear job is easier to test and reuse than repeated inline logic.

sections.title: Three common function forms
sections.body: A declaration uses function name() and is available throughout its scope. A function expression stores a function value in a binding. An arrow function is shorter and is common for callbacks; a concise arrow returns its expression automatically, while a block body needs an explicit return.

sections.title: Arrow functions do not create this
sections.body: A normal function’s this depends on how it is called. An arrow function captures this from the surrounding scope and cannot be used as a constructor. This makes arrows useful for callbacks, but a method that needs the receiving object may need normal method syntax.

sections.title: Functions are values
sections.body: JavaScript functions can be stored, passed, and returned. addEventListener("click", save) passes save for later; addEventListener("click", save()) calls it now and passes its result. React event props use the same distinction.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Function declarations and arrow functions is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain function declarations and arrow functions to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Explain what a function receives, does, and returns. Write declarations, expressions, and arrow functions. Understand the important arrow-function difference. Pass a function without calling it early.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using function declarations and arrow functions behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can function declarations and arrow functions affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using function declarations and arrow functions produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
